props.title: Everyone Says I Love You
props.initialSlug: Woody Allen's charming musical-comedy of family romance

sections.content: Woody Allen's charming musical experiment **Everyone Says I Love You** (1996) stands unique in both his filmography and 90s cinema. Unlike polished musicals like **Chicago** (2002) or **Moulin Rouge!** (2001), Allen used the actual singing voices of his cast (except Drew Barrymore), creating an endearing amateur quality that fits the film's celebration of everyday romance. The film follows an upper-class Manhattan family through various romantic entanglements across New York, Paris, and Venice, with characters spontaneously breaking into classic standards like "Just You, Just Me" and "I'm Through With Love."

sections.content: Allen's film revived the fantasy musical tradition of **Top Hat** (1935) and **An American in Paris** (1951), where dance numbers emerge organically from everyday moments. The scene where Goldie Hawn floats along the Seine with Allen perfectly captures this magical realism. Yet the film also subverts musical conventions through its deliberately unpolished performances and neurotic Woody Allen dialogue, creating an interesting tension between fantasy and his typical relationship anxiety.

The film's use of location shooting in three iconic cities recalls classic romantic musicals like **On the Town** (1949) and **Funny Face** (1957). But Allen updates this tradition with his contemporary perspective on relationships, wealth, and family dynamics. The ensemble cast, including Edward Norton, Julia Roberts, and Alan Alda, brings both comic timing and surprising musical charm to their performances. SUBHEAD: The Musical Revival Context

sections.content: **Everyone Says I Love You** arrived during a relative drought for movie musicals, years before the genre's resurgence with **Moulin Rouge!** (2001) and **Chicago** (2002). Its casual approach to breaking into song influenced later unconventional musicals like **Romance & Cigarettes** (2005) and **Once** (2007). The film demonstrates how the musical format can work with contemporary storytelling without relying on elaborate production numbers or professional singers.
